sections.title: The DoD model compared with OSI

blocks.text: The DoD model is a condensed version of the OSI model with four layers instead of seven. It is the model the TCP/IP protocol suite was built on, so the two are often used interchangeably in conversation.
Only the middle two map one to one: Host-to-Host is Transport and Internet is Network. The top DoD layer swallows three OSI layers and the bottom one swallows two.

sections.title: Straight-through or crossover: the real rule

blocks.text: An Ethernet port either transmits on pins 1 and 2 and receives on 3 and 6 (MDI, used by PCs, servers, and routers) or the reverse (MDI-X, used by switches and hubs). A link works only when one side's transmit pair lands on the other side's receive pair.

items: Unlike devices (one MDI, one MDI-X): straight-through cable. The switch or hub port already does the crossing.
Like devices (both MDI or both MDI-X): crossover cable, which swaps pins 1 and 2 with 3 and 6.
A straight-through cable has the same standard on both ends (T568B to T568B, or T568A to T568A). A crossover has T568A on one end and T568B on the other.

blocks.text: The whiteboard shortcut uses each device's OSI layer: router 3, switch 2, hub 1. Even to odd is straight-through, odd to odd is crossover, same layer is crossover, with PC to hub as the only exception (straight-through).

The shortcut gets two pairs wrong. Router to hub is odd to odd, but it uses straight-through, the same as PC to hub. Switch to hub is even to odd, but it uses crossover. Fix: count the hub as a switch. Then PCs and routers are one group, switches and hubs are the other, and different groups use straight-through while the same group uses crossover.

items: Shortcut still correct for: PC to switch, router to switch, switch to switch, router to router, PC to router, PC to PC, hub to hub.
Memory hook: PCs and routers talk like computers (MDI). Switches and hubs are the middlemen (MDI-X). Different jobs, straight cable. Same job, cross the cable.
Auto-MDIX (automatic medium-dependent interface crossover) lets a port detect the pairs and swap transmit and receive internally, so most modern gigabit ports work with either cable.
Without Auto-MDIX, the wrong cable means transmit meets transmit. The link light stays off. N10-009 objective 5.2 calls this TX/RX transposed.

Gigabit Ethernet uses all four pairs. A full gigabit crossover also swaps pins 4 and 5 with 7 and 8, but Auto-MDIX is required by the 1000BASE-T standard, so in practice a straight-through cable works.
Packet Tracer and the exam can still test the cable rule even when the gear would bring the link up on its own.
Recite the OSI layers both ways: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away (1 to 7) and All People Seem To Need Data Processing (7 to 1).
Match each PDU to its layer: segment 4, packet 3, frame 2, bits 1.
Map DoD to OSI: Process/Application 5 to 7, Host-to-Host 4, Internet 3, Network Access 1 and 2.
Unlike devices use straight-through; like devices use crossover. PCs and routers are MDI; switches and hubs are MDI-X.

title: Layer 2 Switches, Layer 3 Switches, and Routers
summary: What a Layer 2 switch, a Layer 3 (multilayer) switch, and a router each look at, what they change in a frame or packet, how a Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs with SVIs, and when you still need a router.

items: 1.1 OSI reference model: Layer 2 Data Link and Layer 3 Network.
1.2 Networking appliances: router and switch (physical and virtual).
2.1 Routing technologies: static and dynamic routing, the routing table.
2.2 Switching technologies: VLAN, VLAN database, switch virtual interface (SVI), 802.1Q tagging.
Related notes: Chapter 11 (switching and VLANs) and Chapter 9 (IP routing).

sections.title: Three devices, one question: what do they read?

blocks.text: Every forwarding device answers the same question: where does this go next? The difference is which address it reads to decide, and which table it looks it up in.

rows: Collision domains (every port); one broadcast domain per VLAN
Connects hosts in the same subnet or VLAN at the access layer
MAC inside a VLAN; destination IP between VLANs
MAC address table plus a routing table
Collision domains and broadcast domains (one per VLAN or routed port)
Fast inter-VLAN routing in the distribution or core layer
Joins different networks: LAN to WAN, edge to the internet, NAT and VPN

blocks.text: A Layer 2 switch never reads the IP address to make a forwarding decision. If the destination is in a different subnet, a Layer 2 switch alone cannot get it there: something at Layer 3 (a router or a Layer 3 switch) must route it.

sections.title: How a Layer 2 switch forwards a frame

items: 1. Learn: record the frame's source MAC address and the port it arrived on in the MAC address table.
2. Look up: find the destination MAC address in the table.
3. Forward or filter: send the frame out the one port that matches. If the destination is on the same port it came in on, drop it (filter).
4. Flood: if the destination MAC is unknown, or the frame is a broadcast (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF), send it out every port in that VLAN except the one it came in on.

blocks.text: A Layer 2 switch does not change the frame. The source MAC, destination MAC, IP addresses, and TTL leave exactly as they arrived (an 802.1Q tag may be added or removed on a trunk, but the addresses stay the same).

Because a Layer 2 switch floods broadcasts to every port in a VLAN, the whole VLAN is one broadcast domain. VLANs are how you split a Layer 2 switch into several broadcast domains, and traffic between those VLANs needs routing.

sections.title: How a Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs

blocks.text: A Layer 3 switch is a switch with a routing engine built into its hardware. It still switches frames inside each VLAN at Layer 2. For each VLAN you create a switch virtual interface (SVI), a virtual Layer 3 interface with an IP address, and hosts in that VLAN use the SVI as their default gateway.

items: 1. Host A (VLAN 10, 10.1.10.20) wants Host B (VLAN 20, 10.1.20.30). B is in a different subnet, so A sends the frame to its default gateway: the destination MAC is the VLAN 10 SVI's MAC.
2. The switch sees its own MAC as the destination, so it hands the packet to the routing engine.
3. The routing engine looks up 10.1.20.30 in the routing table and finds the directly connected VLAN 20 network.
4. It decrements the TTL by 1 and recalculates the IPv4 header checksum.
5. It builds a new Layer 2 header: source MAC is the VLAN 20 SVI, destination MAC is Host B (found with ARP).
6. The frame is switched out the VLAN 20 port toward Host B.

blocks.text: When traffic is routed, the MAC addresses change at every hop and the TTL goes down by one. The source and destination IP addresses stay the same (unless NAT is involved). This is true for a router and for a Layer 3 switch.

An SVI is up only when the VLAN exists and at least one port in that VLAN (or a trunk carrying it) is up.
no switchport turns a physical port into a routed port, which acts like a router interface (useful for an uplink to an edge router).

blocks.text: Exam trap: a Layer 3 switch can route, but it usually does not replace the edge router. Features such as NAT to the internet, site-to-site VPN, and WAN interfaces are router (or firewall) jobs in most designs.

Inter-VLAN routing can be done two ways. With router-on-a-stick, one router interface connects to a switch trunk and uses an 802.1Q subinterface per VLAN; all routed traffic crosses that one link and back. With a Layer 3 switch, each VLAN gets an SVI and routing happens inside the switch, which scales much better.

blocks.text: TCP/IP is a suite named after its two most important protocols. IP gets a packet to the right host; TCP or UDP gets the data to the right application on that host using a port number.

rows: Decremented by 1 at every router hop; the packet is dropped at 0 and the router sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message (this is how traceroute works)
Which protocol is inside: 1 ICMP, 6 TCP, 17 UDP, 47 GRE, 50 ESP, 51 AH

blocks.text: IP is connectionless and best effort: it does not promise delivery or order. Reliability, if it is needed, comes from TCP above it.

HTTP/HTTPS, SSH, SMTP, FTP, RDP, SMB, LDAP

blocks.text: Pick UDP when speed and low overhead matter more than guaranteed delivery (voice, video, quick request/response like DNS). Pick TCP when every byte must arrive in order (web pages, file transfers, email).

items: 1. SYN: the client sends SYN with its initial sequence number, for example seq=100.
2. SYN/ACK: the server replies with its own sequence number (seq=300) and acknowledges the client's (ack=101).
3. ACK: the client acknowledges the server (seq=101, ack=301). The connection is established and data can flow.

blocks.text: The acknowledgment number is always the next byte the receiver expects: the other side's sequence number plus the bytes received (a SYN or FIN counts as one).

items: Graceful close: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK (each side closes its own direction, so it takes four segments).
RST (reset) aborts a connection at once, for example when a port is closed or a firewall rejects it.
If an ACK does not arrive in time, TCP retransmits the segment.

blocks.text: Exam trap: the handshake is SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK. Host 1 sends SYN, Host 2 sends SYN/ACK, Host 1 sends the final ACK. A flood of SYNs that never complete is a SYN flood (a denial-of-service attack).
A socket is an IP address plus a port, for example 192.168.1.20:51544 talking to 203.0.113.10:443. The client picks a random ephemeral source port; the server listens on the well-known port.

title: HTML and HTTP: What a Browser Actually Gets
summary: Supplemental: what happens between typing a URL and seeing a page (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP), HTTP methods and status codes, and the HTML a server sends back, so you can tell a network fault from a web page fault.

items: 1.1 OSI reference model: HTTP is a Layer 7 (Application) protocol.
1.4 Ports and protocols: HTTP 80 and HTTPS 443 over TCP.
5.0 Troubleshooting: telling a DNS, connection, or TLS problem apart from a server or page problem.

blocks.text: Supplemental: HTML itself is not an N10-009 exam objective. It is here so you can see what the Application layer actually carries and read a status code like a technician.

sections.title: From URL to page, step by step

items: 1. DNS: the browser resolves the host name (www.example.com) to an IP address, usually over UDP 53.
2. TCP: it opens a connection to that IP on port 443 with the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK).
3. TLS: client and server agree on encryption and the server proves its identity with a certificate.
4. HTTP request: the browser sends GET / with headers such as Host and User-Agent.
5. HTTP response: the server returns a status line (HTTP/1.1 200 OK), headers (Content-Type: text/html), and the HTML body.
6. Render: the browser parses the HTML into a DOM tree, then makes more requests for the CSS, JavaScript, and images the HTML points to.

blocks.text: Each failure shows up differently. DNS failure: the name cannot be resolved. TCP failure: connection refused or timed out. TLS failure: a certificate warning. Server reached but page missing: an HTTP status code such as 404.

sections.title: Public, private, APIPA, and loopback addresses

items: Public addresses are routable on the Internet. Private addresses (RFC 1918) are not.
Class A private range: 10.0.0.0 through 10.255.255.255.
Class B private range: 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255.
Class C private range: 192.168.0.0 through 192.168.255.255.

APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) range: 169.254.0.1 through 169.254.255.254. A client that cannot reach a DHCP server configures itself with an APIPA address and the default Class B mask 255.255.0.0.
Loopback (localhost) addresses point a host at itself. 127.0.0.1 is the one you use.

blocks.text: Seeing 169.254.x.x on a client means DHCP did not answer. It is a symptom to troubleshoot, not an address to keep.

items: The gap between 126 and 128 is the 127 loopback network.
Class D and E have no network and host split because they are not used for ordinary host addressing.

sections.title: Which private range should you use?

items: For a corporate network of any size, consultants use a Class A private network (10.0.0.0) because it gives the most flexibility and room to grow.
Example: Acme Corporation has 14 departments with about 70 users each. A plan of 10.1.x.0 with a /24 mask, where x is the department's subnet number, is easy to design, install, and troubleshoot.
Using 10.0.0.0 with a /24 mask gives 65,536 networks of 254 hosts each.
For a home network, use a Class C private address. It is the easiest to understand and configure, and the default Class C mask gives one network with 254 hosts.

CIDR and VLSM let you give each department or building only the number of addresses it needs, without wasting space. Chapter 8 covers the subnet math. A /24 means 24 of the 32 mask bits are turned on.

sections.title: Why IPv6, and how it differs

items: Without IPv6 the world would run out of IPv4 addresses. IPv6 mitigates address exhaustion.
An IPv6 address is 128 bits long and written in hexadecimal. An IPv4 address is 32 bits long and written in decimal.
If the acronym IP is used alone, it means IPv4.
Link-local addresses are like IPv4 APIPA addresses, but they cannot be routed at all, not even inside your organization.
Unique local addresses are like IPv4 private addresses. They cannot be routed to the Internet, but unlike link-local they can be routed inside your organization.

blocks.text: Link-local: never routed. Unique local: routed inside the organization, never on the Internet.

rows: One-to-one: a packet goes to a single interface
An address assigned to one interface
Used just like a regular public, routable IPv4 address
Always starts with FE80::/10. Not meant to be routed
Starts with FC00::/7. Not routed to the Internet but still globally unique. Used to be called site-local
One-to-nearest: identifies multiple interfaces, delivered only to the first one it finds

items: IPv6 has 128-bit addresses against 32-bit IPv4 addresses, so 96 more bits.
Benefits over IPv4 include more available addresses, a simpler header, and options for authentication and other security.
A MAC address is a 48-bit (6-byte) address physically assigned to a network interface such as a NIC. It is also called a hardware address or a burned-in address.

blocks.text: Match the phrase to the type: single interface is unicast, public-like is global unicast, not routed is link-local, not on the Internet but globally unique is unique local, multiple interfaces is multicast, nearest is anycast.

sections.title: IPv6 compatibility: tunneling, dual stack, NAT64

items: Tunneling carries IPv6 traffic inside IPv4 so it can cross an IPv4-only part of the network.
Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 side by side on the same devices.
NAT64 translates between IPv6 and IPv4 so IPv6-only hosts can reach IPv4 services.
Hosts can use stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) to obtain an IPv6 address without a DHCP server. One way to build the interface ID is EUI-64.
EUI-64 takes the host's 48-bit MAC address and inserts FF:FE in the middle, which makes a 64-bit interface ID.
It also inverts the 7th bit of the first byte, typically changing it from 0 to 1.

title: IP Subnetting, Troubleshooting IP, and NAT
summary: Why you subnet, default masks and CIDR, the big five subnetting questions, worked /25 example, Class C mask table, classful vs classless and VLSM, the /30 WAN mask, and an introduction to NAT and PAT.

items: Domain 1.0 Networking Concepts, 1.4: explain common networking ports, protocols, services, and traffic types. Traffic types are unicast, multicast, anycast, and broadcast.

Domain 1.0 Networking Concepts, 1.7: use appropriate IPv4 network addressing. This covers public vs. private (APIPA, RFC 1918, loopback/localhost), subnetting (VLSM and CIDR), and IPv4 address classes A to E.
Domain 2.0 Network Implementation, 2.1: explain characteristics of routing technologies, including address translation with NAT and port address translation (PAT).
Add a router to a physical network and you have an internetwork. The hosts on it must now have a logical network addressing scheme to communicate.
IPv6 could be used, but IPv4 is still the most popular, and it is what this chapter covers.
The key to understanding subnetting is understanding the very reason you need to do it. Subnetting splits one network into smaller networks, so each segment on a router gets its own network ID.

sections.title: Default subnet masks and CIDR notation

items: CIDR notation writes how many bits of the mask are turned on, after a slash. 255.255.255.0 has 24 bits on, so it is /24.
The network ID is the part of the address covered by the mask. The host ID is the rest.
1. How many subnets? 2 to the power of the number of subnet bits (mask bits turned on in the interesting octet). For 255.255.255.128 that is 1 bit, so 2^1 = 2.

2. How many hosts per subnet? 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2. For /25 there are 7 host bits, so 2^7 - 2 = 126. The 2 removed are the subnet address (all host bits off) and the broadcast address (all host bits on).
3. What are the valid subnets? Block size = 256 minus the mask value in the interesting octet. 256 - 128 = 128. Start at zero and count in the block size: 0, 128.
4. What is the broadcast address of each subnet? The number right before the next subnet, with all host bits turned on. The next subnet after 0 is 128, so the broadcast of the 0 subnet ends in 127.
5. What are the valid hosts? The numbers between the subnet address and its broadcast address.

blocks.text: Write the subnet address and the broadcast address first. The valid hosts are then obvious: everything in between.
Network address 192.168.10.0 with subnet mask 255.255.255.128 (/25). The number 128 is 10000000 in binary, so 1 bit is used for subnetting and 7 bits are left for hosts.
/25 on a Class C gives 2 subnets with 126 hosts each. Subnets: 0 and 128. Broadcasts: 127 and 255.

sections.title: Class C masks at a glance

blocks.text: The same five steps work for every Class C mask. Compare each row with the /25 example.
Quick check: subnets times block size always equals 256 in a Class C network.

items: A classful network uses the same subnet mask on every host and router interface.
Classless routing lets you use different size masks in the same network. Giving each link a mask that fits its need is called variable length subnet masking (VLSM).
CIDR (classless inter-domain routing) is the slash notation used to write those masks, such as /25 or /30.

sections.title: Real world: the /30 mask for WAN links

items: Scenario: you administer Acme Corporation in San Francisco with dozens of WAN links to the corporate office. Every host and router interface uses the same mask, and you must pick a mask for point-to-point links.
A /24 (255.255.255.0) gives each WAN network 254 hosts, but a WAN link uses only 2 addresses. That wastes 252 addresses per link.
A /30 (255.255.255.252) leaves 2 host bits, so 2^2 - 2 = 2 hosts per subnet. That is exactly enough for the two ends of a link, and no precious addresses are wasted.

blocks.text: Point-to-point WAN links: use 255.255.255.252 (/30). Two usable hosts, nothing wasted.

A routing loop sends packets around a set of routers without ever reaching the destination. Each hop lowers the TTL, and the packet is dropped when TTL reaches 0.

Split horizon is a loop-prevention rule used by distance-vector protocols such as RIP and IGRP. A router does not advertise a route back out the interface it learned that route on.

summary: Recognize attack mechanisms, explain their impact, and choose layered defenses from evidence rather than a single symptom. Includes original scenarios and a paper incident exercise.

It also develops selected 4.1 concepts (physical security, deception, segmentation) and 4.3 defenses. It complements the existing security and risk notes; it is not a complete security configuration course.

items: Explain what the attacker changes: availability, address bindings, name resolution, trust, or human decisions.

A denial-of-service attack prevents legitimate use by exhausting bandwidth, connection state, processing capacity, or another resource. A distributed attack uses multiple sources. Reflection and amplification describe mechanisms, so an attack can be distributed, reflected, and amplified at the same time.

rows: One source or many sources send disruptive traffic or requests.
Legitimate traffic loses capacity; compare utilization and service logs, then coordinate filtering and upstream mitigation.
Requests carry the victim’s spoofed source address; third-party servers reply to the victim.
Reply traffic reaches a host that did not request it; restrict exposed reflectors and apply source-address validation at network boundaries.
A request induces a larger response or repeated responses.
A small attack input creates greater victim load. DNS and vulnerable NTP services can be abused; amplification is not a fixed number of megabytes.

blocks.text: Botnets can receive command-and-control (C2) instructions, but C2 also supports other malware activity. Neither a C2 connection nor an outage alone proves DDoS. A local firewall cannot recover an upstream link already saturated; involve the provider and incident-response team. Equipment theft or destructive firmware changes can also deny service, but they are mechanisms with different evidence, not proof of a packet flood.

A switch normally learns source MAC addresses and forwards using destination MAC addresses. MAC flooding feeds many fabricated source addresses into the learning process to pressure the forwarding table. Unknown destinations may then be flooded within a VLAN, exposing traffic or consuming capacity. Exact overflow behavior depends on the switch; it does not guarantee access to every frame or every VLAN.

VLAN hopping attempts to cross a VLAN boundary without the intended routed policy. Switch spoofing abuses unwanted trunk negotiation. Double tagging can expose an inner VLAN tag after the outer native-VLAN tag is removed along a susceptible trunk path. It depends on topology and tagging behavior; it is not a universal two-way session or a synonym for all VLAN hopping.

items: Keep user ports explicitly in access mode and disable unwanted trunk negotiation where supported.
Use a native VLAN not assigned to user access ports, consistent trunk settings, and appropriate allowed-VLAN restrictions. Verify current platform guidance before changing tagging.
Port-security MAC limits can reduce address-table abuse; violation actions and support vary. MAC addresses can be spoofed, so an allowed address is not strong identity proof.

sections.title: ARP spoofing, poisoning, and MAC spoofing

blocks.text: ARP resolves an IPv4 address to a link-layer address on the local network. Forged ARP messages can claim that the gateway’s IP belongs to the attacker’s MAC. Spoofing describes the false claim; poisoning describes the resulting false cache binding. These terms commonly overlap.

Changing an interface to use somebody else’s MAC address is MAC spoofing. It is not, by itself, ARP poisoning. ARP poisoning requires false address-resolution information; the attacker can retain their own MAC while claiming the gateway’s IP.

The resulting traffic redirection can enable interception, manipulation, or a black hole. Compare the gateway binding with an approved baseline and correlate captures, switch-port data, and change records. Redundancy or a legitimate hardware replacement can also change a binding. Dynamic ARP inspection can validate messages using trusted bindings; DHCP snooping, static hosts, and trusted-port configuration need platform-specific planning.

DNS spoofing supplies a forged name-resolution answer. Cache poisoning leaves false data in a resolver cache, potentially redirecting later clients until the record is removed or expires. A redirected login can steal credentials or interrupt service. A single wrong answer does not establish where the bad information originated.

items: Compare the client’s resolver and response with the approved resolver, authoritative data, and the change history. Preserve evidence before clearing caches.
DNSSEC validation checks signed DNS data for origin authenticity and integrity when a valid trust chain exists. It does not encrypt DNS queries.
Encrypted DNS transports protect a connection to a resolver; they do not make a malicious resolver trustworthy. Validate TLS server identities at the application too.

Clients can be redirected or disconnected. Identify the source port, compare approved scopes, and use correctly configured DHCP snooping where supported.
An unauthorized AP provides wireless access, sometimes through an employee’s wired connection.
It can bypass admission policy. Compare inventory, controller data, and physical findings; remove or isolate it through the response process.
An AP impersonates a legitimate wireless network to attract clients.
It can intercept or redirect sessions. A matching SSID alone proves neither legitimacy nor an attack; legitimate APs share SSIDs. Verify inventory and authentication settings.

blocks.text: An evil twin need not use a particular channel or connect to the victim organization’s wired LAN. A rogue AP need not copy an SSID. Use managed wireless profiles and server-certificate validation for enterprise authentication; do not teach users to ignore certificate errors. Wireless monitoring and physical investigation complement access controls.

sections.title: On-path attacks and the evidence threshold

blocks.text: An on-path attacker is positioned between communicating systems and can relay, observe, or alter traffic. Older sources call this man-in-the-middle. ARP poisoning, malicious DHCP settings, or an evil twin may create that position, but each requires supporting evidence. DNS redirection may instead take the client directly to an impostor service; that alone does not prove transparent relaying.

Correctly validated TLS provides confidentiality and integrity for application data across an untrusted path. It does not fix a compromised endpoint, stop all outages, or legitimize a certificate warning. Stolen credentials from one workstation could result from phishing, malware, credential reuse, or interception. Investigate rather than naming on-path solely from that symptom.

rows: A deceptive message or site prompts a credential entry, payment, or malicious download.
Verify through a separately known channel; report the message; combine training, filtering, updates, and phishing-resistant MFA where available.
Discarded documents or media disclose useful information.
Use approved secure disposal and protect waste containing sensitive material.
Someone observes a screen, keypad, or other sensitive entry.
Shield the entry and screen; control positioning and access.
Someone follows an authorized person through a controlled entrance without independent authorization.
Use visitor procedures and individual access checks; report safely rather than physically confronting someone.

blocks.text: Cameras provide observation and evidence, while locks restrict physical access. Neither replaces a response process. Protect network closets, racks, and exposed jacks. Terms such as piggybacking are used inconsistently across sources; describe whether access was authorized instead of grading solely on that distinction.

Malware is software used for malicious activity. A virus attaches to a host file, a worm can propagate between systems, a Trojan misrepresents its purpose, and spyware or a keylogger can collect information. A bot may receive C2 instructions. These categories can overlap.

Ransomware may encrypt data for extortion and can be accompanied by data theft. Shared storage and reachable systems increase the blast radius. Report and contain according to the incident plan, preserve evidence, and use tested recovery sources; paying or running a cleaner is not a recovery guarantee.

Combine supported endpoint protection, patching, least privilege, segmentation, email/web controls, and tested protected backups. Product labels such as antivirus and antimalware do not prove exact capability. Phishing may involve no malware at all, so no generic endpoint tool guarantees protection against every deceptive message. Changing default passwords removes a known credential; it does not eliminate guessing attacks. Add suitable authentication and rate limiting.

rows: Disable unused ports and services; change defaults
Reduce exposed functions and known credentials.
Keep required management access and a rollback path; update supported software and test authorized functions.
Limit learned addresses or apply an address-based allowlist.
Address spoofing can bypass address-only identity assumptions.
Control network admission using authenticated users or devices through an authenticator and authentication service.
Identity authentication alone does not establish current antivirus or patch status.
Restrict or remediate devices failing defined security checks.
Endpoint agents, supported products, licensing, and enforcement features vary; test noncompliant and compliant devices.
Protect secrets through generation, storage, controlled use, rotation, revocation, and retirement.
Do not share private keys or publish real credentials in a lab; follow the applicable certificate and device lifecycle.

blocks.text: For example, admit an authenticated staff laptop to normal services only after the supported posture check passes; send a noncompliant device to limited remediation services. This is a policy example, not a runnable vendor configuration.

An ACL evaluates traffic against rules such as source, destination, protocol, and transport port. On classic Cisco IOS interface IP ACLs, specify inbound or outbound relative to the interface; one ACL per interface, protocol, and direction is a platform rule, not a universal limit on every ACL. A list can be reused on multiple interfaces. Test rule order, permitted flows, denied flows, return traffic, and logging.

URL filtering controls access based on destinations or URL policy; content filtering evaluates categories or inspected content. Encryption and product capabilities affect visibility. Neither policy name proves all phishing or malware will be blocked.

rows: Visitors and personally owned devices need different access from managed staff systems.
Internet access and required infrastructure only; deny internal administration by default.
Small devices and industrial sensors can have constrained update and authentication options.
Only required collectors and management paths.
Operational technology controls physical processes; industrial control systems and supervisory monitoring have safety and availability constraints.
Approved control or telemetry paths through managed boundaries; coordinate changes with process owners.
Place public-facing services between external and more sensitive internal zones.
Public HTTPS to a web service; only explicitly required backend access.

blocks.text: A VLAN separates broadcast domains. It does not automatically restrict routed traffic. Enforce zone policy with appropriate ACLs/firewalls; “trusted” describes a policy zone, not permission to skip identity checks. Never experiment on production industrial equipment.

A honeypot is a monitored decoy designed to attract suspicious interaction. A honeynet groups decoy systems into a network. They can improve detection and investigation, but do not replace production controls. Isolate them from real assets, restrict outbound access, and assign monitoring and response ownership; do not put real secrets in a decoy.

items: 2.4 GHz has the longest range and the most interference. Non-overlapping channels in the US are 1, 6 and 11. Any other channel overlaps with at least one of them.
5 GHz has more channels and less interference, with shorter range. 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E) adds more spectrum.
Wider channels (40, 80 or 160 MHz) carry more data but pick up more interference. 20 MHz is the standard width.
Band steering moves capable clients from 2.4 GHz to 5 GHz on dual- and tri-band access points.
SSID is the network name; BSSID is one radio's MAC address; ESSID is one logical network across several access points so clients can roam.

rows: Current best practice; resists offline password guessing
Not every older device supports it
Hard to revoke one user; everyone shares the password

Racks are measured in U units, where 1 U is 1.75 inches. A standard rack is 42U.
Switches and routers should match the rack's airflow. In a hot aisle and cold aisle layout, cold air enters the front and hot air exits the back.
Patch panels separate permanent building cable from short patch cables, so you change the patch cable, not the wall run.
Lockable cabling or locking ports prevent accidental or deliberate unplugging in high-security areas.

Rack-mounted power strip that distributes power to the gear

Works when the network is down

Out-of-band management uses a separate path, such as a serial console or a modem line, so you can recover a device during an outage.
A jump box (jump host) is one hardened, monitored entry point. Administrators connect to it first, then move on to internal devices. Protect it with MFA and patching.

rows: More traffic than the link can carry
Buffers fill and packets are dropped
Devices competing for one resource at the same instant
Busy shared link at peak time
One narrow point that limits the whole path

items: Bandwidth is the theoretical maximum of a link. Throughput is what actually moves through it. Over a path, the slowest link sets the throughput.
On wireless: interference from neighboring access points, channel overlap, signal degradation through walls and distance, and dead zones with insufficient coverage.

RSSI measures signal strength at the client; SNR measures signal relative to background noise. Roaming thresholds decide when a client hands off, and a low threshold can leave a client stuck to a distant access point.

blocks.text: Latency is slow, jitter is uneven, and loss means the data is gone. Jitter is what ruins voice calls.

items: Channel overlap: 2.4 GHz has three non-overlapping channels in North America (1, 6 and 11). Nearby access points on overlapping channels interfere with each other.
Insufficient coverage: weak signal in an area. Add or move access points, or add antenna gain.
Client disassociation: clients are dropped from the access point and must reconnect. Look for weak signal, interference or too many clients.
Roaming misconfiguration: a client holds on to a distant access point because roaming thresholds are set badly.
Bottlenecking: the slowest point on the path limits the throughput of the whole transfer.

title: Troubleshooting methodology: the seven steps (5.1)

rows: Gather information, question users, identify symptoms, find out what changed, duplicate the problem if possible, approach multiple problems individually
2. Establish a theory of probable cause
Decide what most likely caused it
Question the obvious, then consider multiple approaches: top-to-bottom, bottom-to-top, divide and conquer
3. Test the theory to determine the cause
If confirmed, decide the next steps. If not, establish a new theory or escalate
Plan the fix before touching production
Identify potential effects, rollback, who is affected, change approval
Make the fix, or hand it to someone with the access or skill
Often done inside an approved maintenance window
Confirm the original problem is gone
Ask the users, check for side effects, add preventive measures where applicable
7. Document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned
Keep notes throughout the process, not only at the end

blocks.text: The exam asks for the order and for which step a described action belongs to. Learn the verbs: identify, theorize, test, plan, implement, verify, document.

items: Step 1 questions: What are the symptoms? Who and how many are affected? Did anything change recently (new device, update, configuration, move)? Can you reproduce it?
If several problems are reported at once, separate them and work each one on its own so the fixes do not get tangled together.
Question the obvious first: is it plugged in, is the link light on, is the port enabled, is the user on the right network?

rows: Start at OSI Layer 1 and work upward
Check cable and link lights, then IP addressing, then the application
Start at Layer 7 and work downward
App fails, so test the application, then the transport port, then the network path
Start at a middle layer, then move up or down depending on the result
Ping the default gateway (Layer 3). Success means look higher. Failure means look lower

items: Test the theory on a non-production system or with a low-risk check when you can. A theory that fails sends you back to step 2, or to escalation if the problem is beyond your access or skill.
The plan of action covers the change itself, the risk, the rollback plan, who is notified and any approval needed.
Escalate when the fault is outside your control, such as an ISP circuit, or needs someone with more authority.
Verify with the people who reported the problem. Preventive measures stop it from returning, such as a monitoring alert or a spare part.

UTP in a noisy area picks up interference. Shielded twisted pair resists it
Use STP, grounded correctly, or reroute

Better category, proper twist, proper termination

items: PoE power budget exceeded: the switch has a total wattage limit. Add up every powered device. If the total goes over, some devices will not power up.
Incorrect PoE standard: 802.3af (PoE), 802.3at (PoE+) and 802.3bt (PoE++) deliver increasing power. A camera that needs PoE+ will not run on a plain PoE port.
An endspan device is the PoE switch itself. A midspan device is an injector placed between a non-PoE switch and the powered device.
Transceiver mismatch: speed, wavelength (for example 850 nm vs 1310 nm), connector or fiber type must match at both ends.
Signal strength: switches can show receive light levels. Low levels point to a dirty connector, a bend, a long run or a failing transceiver.

title: Network services issues: switching, routing and addressing (5.3)
summary: Trace loops, VLAN mistakes, ACLs, routes and IP settings to the right fix.

items: A loop between switches makes frames circle forever. Ethernet frames have no hop count, so the result is a broadcast storm and an overwhelmed network.
Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) prevents loops by blocking redundant paths. Switches exchange BPDUs to learn the topology.
The root bridge is the switch with the lowest bridge ID (priority first, then the lowest MAC address on a tie).
A bad root bridge election, such as a slow access switch becoming root, sends traffic down poor paths. Set the priority on the switch you want.

rows: The best path toward the root bridge
The port that forwards toward the segment, away from the root
Held in reserve to break the loop until another link fails

blocks.text: Port states in classic STP: blocking, listening, learning, forwarding. Only forwarding passes user traffic. Learning builds the MAC address table without forwarding frames.

items: Incorrect VLAN assignment: a device gets an address but cannot reach neighbors because its port is in a different VLAN. Check the port with show vlan or the interface configuration.
ACLs: a rule that denies traffic can break one service or one direction while everything else works. Look at recent ACL changes and rule order.
ACLs are checked from top to bottom and the first match wins. An implicit deny sits at the end.

items: Asset inventory: a central record of hardware and software. It holds model, serial number, asset tag, owner or assigned user, location, purchase date, warranty status, firmware version, and software licenses with versions and expiration dates.
Asset tags: visible labels, often with a barcode or RFID, that tie a device to a ticket, to finance depreciation, and to warranty tracking.

IP address management (IPAM): plans, tracks and configures IPv4 and IPv6 addressing and DHCP and DNS data from one console. It prevents duplicate assignments, shows which user held an address at a given time, and warns when a scope is running out.

rows: How many licenses do we own, and when does the warranty end?
Which address did this laptop hold at 9:15 yesterday?
Is the ISP meeting its promised uptime?

Validating coverage and finding interference or rogue access points
Associate to the network and pass traffic
Measuring real throughput, loss and roaming

title: Life cycle, change and configuration management (3.1)
summary: Plan equipment from purchase to disposal, control changes with a formal process, and keep production, backup and golden configurations.

rows: The vendor stops selling the product
Plan its replacement. Support may continue for a while
The vendor stops patches, fixes and help
Replace or accept the risk. Unpatched devices become security gaps
Tracking OS, firmware and application versions, patches and licenses
Test, schedule and apply updates; remove unlicensed or unsupported software
Back up needed data, wipe it, remove it from inventory, monitoring and DNS, then recycle with records

Change management is the formal process for planning and approving changes so they are scheduled, tested, communicated and reversible. The documentation also helps rebuild a system after a disaster.

items: Request the change and state the reason.
Assess the risk and impact, and plan how to test it.
Get approval, usually from a change advisory board for significant changes.
Schedule it in a maintenance window and notify everyone affected.
Back up first and have a rollback plan.
Implement and verify, then document the result and close the change.

rows: The configuration currently running and the standard for new devices of that kind
A copy saved before a change so it can be restored. A VM snapshot is a backup of the whole machine state
A tested, approved configuration, including hardware, firmware, drivers and software versions, used as the reference

items: Integrity checks compare production to the golden configuration.
A difference means either fix production to match, or approve the change and update the baseline to a new version.
Test in a lab first. Not every case can be tested, so always keep a way to revert.

title: Disaster recovery concepts (3.3)
summary: Set recovery targets with RPO and RTO, judge reliability with MTBF and MTTR, choose a cold, warm or hot site, remove single points of failure, and prove the plan with tests.

blocks.text: Disaster recovery (DR) restores technology after a disruptive event. It is one part of business continuity planning (BCP), which keeps the whole organization working. Recovery targets come from the business, usually from a business impact analysis (BIA) that ranks systems by the cost of losing them.

rows: Backward in time from the failure to the last good copy
Forward in time from the failure until service is back
Recovery site tier and standing redundancy
Average time a component runs before it fails
Average time to restore a failed component

items: An RPO of 1 hour means copies at least hourly. A zero RPO needs synchronous replication.
Set RPO and RTO per system. An order database may need a 5 minute RTO, while an internal wiki can wait two days.
Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). With 1,000 hours between failures and 2 hours to repair, availability is 1000 / 1002, about 99.8 percent.
Cutting MTTR is usually cheaper than raising MTBF: keep spares, test the runbook and buy a fast support contract.

rows: Space, power and connectivity, but no equipment or data
Installed hardware, data restored from backups or periodic replication
Full duplicate with continuously replicated data

items: Pick the tier from the RTO. A tight RTO needs a hot site, a generous one allows a cold site.
A warm site's data refresh interval sets its RPO. Nightly replication means up to 24 hours of loss.
Site resiliency also covers moving back to the primary site (failback) after the disaster.
In the cloud, a pilot light design replicates data continuously but starts compute only at failover.

blocks.text: Cold means bring everything. Warm means bring the data. Hot means just switch.

High availability (HA) removes single points of failure so one failed part does not cause an outage. DR sites answer the loss of a whole site. HA covers an ordinary failed power supply, cable or router.

rows: One device carries traffic. The standby watches it and takes over on failure
Simple, but the standby capacity sits idle
Both devices carry traffic at once, often behind a load balancer
More capacity, but needs careful design, and each device must be able to carry the full load alone

items: Active-passive pairs must share identical configuration and synchronize state such as session and routing tables, so the standby behaves the same after takeover.
Two active nodes each at 70 percent load cannot cover each other: the survivor would face 140 percent.
Redundancy is layered: dual power supplies, NIC teaming to two switches, first-hop redundancy protocols at the gateway, and load balancing.

rows: The team talks through a scenario using the plan, and no systems are touched
None. Finds missing contacts, roles and dependencies
Real recovery steps are run to prove the technology works
Bring the DR site up beside live production and confirm services work
Switch production to the DR site, then fail back
Highest, but the only real measure of RTO and RPO

summary: Separate the data, control and management planes, see why SD-WAN suits cloud traffic, and learn how VXLAN overlays stretch layer 2 across routed networks and data centers.

blocks.text: A router, switch or firewall does three jobs. Software-defined networking (SDN) separates them so the logic can run as software and be managed centrally.

rows: Forwards traffic from one interface to another
Routing tables, switching tables, NAT tables
How administrators configure and monitor the device

blocks.text: SD-WAN applies the same idea to the wide area network. Applications moved from one data center to SaaS and IaaS, so branches need to reach many cloud locations, not only headquarters.

rows: Recognizes the application and sends it by the best path, such as email straight to the nearest cloud service
A new edge device configures itself when it connects, without a technician on site
Works over fiber, broadband, 5G or DSL, as long as there is IP reachability
Policies are set once on a controller and pushed to every edge device

items: Network function virtualization (NFV) replaces dedicated appliances with virtual firewalls, routers or load balancers on standard servers.
Local breakout lets a branch reach cloud services directly instead of hairpinning through the headquarters firewall.

blocks.text: An overlay is a network built from tunnels across another network, the underlay. The underlay only delivers packets and never reads what is inside them. VXLAN is the data center overlay.

rows: Carries Ethernet (layer 2) frames inside UDP/IP packets, so a layer 2 segment can exist anywhere IP reaches
VXLAN tunnel endpoint. Usually a leaf switch or hypervisor virtual switch that adds and removes the VXLAN header
VXLAN network identifier. 24 bits, about 16 million segments, compared with 4,096 for a 12-bit VLAN ID
About 50 bytes per packet, so the underlay needs a larger MTU, such as jumbo frames

items: Data center interconnect (DCI) joins data centers so workloads can fail over or move and keep their IP addresses.
Stretching VLANs over dark fiber makes spanning tree and broadcast storms span both sites. VXLAN over a routed link keeps failures contained.
VXLAN does not encrypt. Add IPsec on untrusted links.
When an overlay fails, check the underlay first. A single link with a small MTU lets small packets pass but stalls large transfers.

title: Zero trust, SASE, infrastructure as code and IPv6 transition (1.8)
summary: Apply zero trust principles, tell SASE from SSE, use templates, playbooks and Git for automation, and pick dual stack, tunneling or NAT64 for IPv6 coexistence.

blocks.text: The old perimeter model trusted anything inside the firewall. Zero trust removes that assumption: every request is evaluated on its own, using identity, device posture, resource and context.

rows: Authenticate and authorize each request, with stronger checks for riskier context, such as MFA on an unmanaged device
Give one user access to one resource for one session, not the whole network
Design as if an attacker is already inside: segment, monitor and contain

items: The policy decision point (PDP) evaluates the request against policy. The policy enforcement point (PEP) allows or blocks the connection.
Verification is continuous. A device that stops complying loses access during the session.
ZTNA connects a user to one application and hides everything else. A classic VPN puts the device on the whole internal network.
Microsegmentation applies policy to each server, VM or container, so every lateral hop is blocked and logged.

rows: Cloud-delivered security: secure web gateway (SWG), cloud access security broker (CASB), ZTNA and firewall as a service (FWaaS)
SSE plus SD-WAN, delivered from provider points of presence near users

A parallel line of work so main is never edited directly

Distribution and core combined into one layer or pair of switches
Small and medium networks. Lower cost, with more responsibility on one block

Data centers. Predictable latency, easy growth by adding leaves or spines

A top-of-rack switch is the leaf for the servers in its rack.

Four lanes of 10 Gbps in one port
Four lanes of 25 Gbps in one port

Cheap, low power and low latency. Transceivers are built into the cable ends

summary: Choose between site-to-site, client-to-site and clientless VPNs, split and full tunnels, SSH, GUI, API, console and jump boxes, and in-band vs out-of-band management.

blocks.text: A VPN builds an encrypted tunnel across a network you do not trust, usually the internet. It protects the path between its two endpoints. It does not make the user anonymous or fix a compromised device.

rows: Always on and transparent to users. Usually IPsec. The two sides must not use overlapping address space
One device to the corporate network

One user's browser to selected web applications

Full inspection and logging, but more load and latency at headquarters
Only traffic for the corporate network uses the VPN
Faster, but the organization cannot see the internet traffic and the device bridges both networks

rows: Encrypted command line. Supports key-based authentication, SFTP and tunneling. The everyday secure choice
Same job in clear text. Do not use it
Web interface for occasional tasks and viewing device state
For automation and monitoring. Scriptable and consistent
Needs no IP address or working configuration. Used for first setup and recovery. You must be present or use a console server
Graphical remote desktop. RDP is Microsoft. VNC works across platforms. Do not expose to the internet

items: A jump box (jump server or bastion host) is a hardened host that is the single entry point for administration of a sensitive segment. Admins connect to it first, it is logged, and the protected systems accept management only from it. It sits at the edge or in a DMZ and is a single point of compromise, so it is hardened more than anything it protects.
A console server (terminal server) gives network access to many devices' serial console ports, usually 8, 16 or 32 ports in a 1U unit. KVM over IP does the same for keyboard, video and mouse.

rows: The production network that carries user data
Cheap and simple, but fails when the network fails
A separate dedicated path, such as a console server on its own network, often with a cellular uplink
Still works when the production network is down or misconfigured

items: Network down: console or out-of-band.
Automation: API.
Graphical desktop: through a VPN or jump box.
Otherwise: SSH.

summary: A grouped reference of well-known TCP and UDP ports by purpose, with secure and insecure pairs, plus ports that signal trouble.

UDP for queries. TCP for large responses and zone transfers
UDP. 161 queries to agents, 162 traps to the manager

blocks.text: The secure version of a mail protocol is nearly always in the 990s (993, 995) or 465/587 for submission.

title: Network monitoring technologies (3.2)
summary: Read SNMP, flow data, packet captures, syslog and SIEM correctly, tell SPAN from a TAP, and use baselines and alerts to catch problems early.

Software on a managed device that answers requests and sends alerts
The agent's catalog of monitorable values, organized as a tree
Dotted-number address of one value in the MIB. Vendor-specific values sit in vendor branches
Manager reads one value, the next value, or many values (UDP 161)
Agent sends an unsolicited alert the moment an event happens (UDP 162)
Community string in clear text, plus bulk retrieval and 64-bit counters
Per-user authentication, integrity and encryption. Use auth-priv in production

Security levels in v3: no auth/no priv, auth/no priv, auth/priv (authentication and encryption).

rows: Summary of conversations: addresses, ports, protocol, bytes, packets, duration. No payload
Who is using bandwidth, long-term trends
Detailed troubleshooting and protocol analysis. Fills storage quickly
Copies traffic from ports or VLANs to a monitoring port
Flexible capture, but can drop copies when busy and does not copy bad frames
Hardware inserted in the link that copies all traffic, including errors
Accurate capture that does not depend on switch load

items: Syslog default transport is UDP 514, which has no retransmission. TCP syslog or syslog over TLS is preferred when completeness or confidentiality matters.
Each syslog message has a facility and a severity from 0 to 7: 0 emergency, 1 alert, 2 critical, 3 error, 4 warning, 5 notice, 6 informational, 7 debug. A lower number is more urgent.
A device configured for level 4 sends levels 0 to 4 and discards the rest. Production commonly sends level 6 and above.

Log aggregation forwards all device logs to a central collector because local buffers are small, a failed or compromised device loses its log, and incidents span many devices. Synchronize time with NTP first.
A SIEM correlates events from many sources. A firewall deny, repeated login failures and a new admin account are routine alone but signal a compromise together.

blocks.text: Mnemonic for severity 0 to 7: Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Ice cream Daily.

rows: Time for data to travel from source to destination
Variation in latency. Matters for voice and video
Percentage of packets that never arrive
CRC errors, collisions and other interface problems
Temperature, humidity, water and door sensors

items: A baseline records normal behavior, including daily and monthly patterns. Re-establish it after a legitimate change.
A fixed threshold, such as 80 percent utilization, false-alarms on normal peaks and misses anomalies during quiet hours. Anomaly alerting compares each metric with what is expected for that time.
API integration and streaming telemetry push structured data, even sub-second, from controllers and cloud platforms. SNMP remains the universal baseline for physical equipment.
Good alerting is actionable, routed by severity, aware of dependencies and has an owner and a runbook. Too many false positives cause alert fatigue.
Network discovery finds devices on demand or on a schedule.

title: DNS records, zones and secure DNS (3.4)
summary: Know what each DNS record type answers, how zones and authority work, and which control fixes which DNS attack: DNSSEC for authenticity, DoT and DoH for privacy.

blocks.text: Every DNS record has five fields: name, TTL, class, type and value. The TTL is how many seconds a resolver may cache the answer. The type decides how the value is read.

rows: Several A records for one name give round-robin DNS: load spreading with no health check
Dual-stack hosts prefer IPv6, so a AAAA record with no working IPv6 path breaks the service
Value is a name, never an address. A name with a CNAME cannot hold other records, so the zone apex cannot be a CNAME
Lowest preference number wins. Target must be a name with an A or AAAA record, never a CNAME
Free text, now mostly email policy
SPF (allowed senders, only one record), DKIM (public key for signatures), DMARC (what to do on failure), domain ownership proof
The list in the zone and at the parent delegation must agree
Primary server, admin email (first dot stands for @), serial number, refresh timers
Lives in a reverse zone, not created with the A record. Mail servers check it
Used to find VoIP, messaging and directory services

blocks.text: Mail rejected even though A and MX look right? Add the PTR record for the sending address. It is usually controlled by the ISP.

items: A zone is the part of the name space one set of servers manages. A delegated subdomain ends the parent zone.
A forward zone maps names to addresses. A reverse zone maps addresses to names with PTR records under in-addr.arpa, with the octets written backwards.
A primary server holds the editable copy. A secondary holds a read-only copy from a zone transfer, and its answers are equally authoritative.
The secondary compares the SOA serial. A higher serial triggers a transfer. Edit a zone without raising the serial and the secondaries keep the old data.
AXFR copies the whole zone, IXFR sends only changes, and both use TCP 53. Unrestricted transfers reveal every host name.
An authoritative answer comes from a server that holds the zone. A non-authoritative answer comes from a resolver cache and can be stale until the TTL expires.
Troubleshooting: query the authoritative server for what the record says, then the resolver for what users see. If they differ, the cache is stale. If both are wrong, edit the record.

rows: Query a name, record type or specific server
Clear the local resolver cache on Windows
Local name entries checked before DNS

blocks.text: Classic DNS has no authentication and no encryption, so a resolver accepts the first plausible reply. That creates two separate problems: are the answers genuine, and are the queries private?

rows: A forged reply arrives before the real one
The same forgery is planted in a resolver, so every client of that resolver gets the fake entry until the TTL expires
The victim is pointed at a different resolver through malware, a compromised router or a rogue DHCP server
Authenticity and integrity: records are signed, and a chain of DS records leads up to the root trust anchor
Encrypted queries on TCP 853. Still recognizable as DNS, so it can be managed or blocked
Proof that the answer is true
Encrypted queries inside normal web traffic on TCP 443. Can bypass enterprise filtering and monitoring
Proof that the answer is true

blocks.text: If DNSSEC signatures expire, validating resolvers return SERVFAIL while non-validating resolvers still answer. Correct records on the authoritative server plus failures only at validating resolvers points to the signatures.

title: DHCP, IPAM and time protocols (3.4)
summary: Follow DHCP from DORA to renewal, fix the scope, relay and rogue-server problems, compare SLAAC with DHCPv6, and choose between NTP, PTP and NTS.

rows: Client has no address, sends from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255
Client broadcasts its choice, so other servers withdraw their offers

items: DHCP uses UDP. The server listens on 67 and the client on 68.
Renewal starts at T1 (50 percent of the lease) with a unicast request to the same server. If that fails, the client broadcasts at T2 (87.5 percent). Only at expiry does it restart the full exchange.
A scope is the range one server may hand out on one subnet. One scope per subnet, each with its own mask, gateway, DNS servers and lease time.
An exclusion removes addresses from the pool so static devices (gateways, servers) are never handed out. Without it you get duplicate address conflicts.

A reservation ties an address to a client MAC address. The device always gets the same address through DHCP and still picks up gateway and DNS changes. New hardware means a new MAC and a broken reservation.
Short leases suit guest Wi-Fi and high-turnover networks. Long leases suit stable wired networks. Scope exhaustion shows as new devices failing while existing ones keep working.

rows: TFTP server and boot file for network booting
TFTP server used by many VoIP phones

items: DHCP starts with a broadcast and routers do not forward broadcasts. A relay agent on the client's default gateway turns the broadcast into a unicast to the server.
Configure the IP helper address on the client-facing interface, naming the server. Putting it on the server-facing interface is the common mistake.
The relay writes its receiving interface address into the gateway IP address field, and the server uses that field to pick the scope.
APIPA, 169.254.0.0/16, means the client got no DHCP reply. The NIC works. The fault is between the client and the server: cable, VLAN, relay, exhausted scope or a down server.
One VLAN gets APIPA while every other VLAN works: check the helper address on that VLAN's interface, then the scope for that subnet, then UDP 67 through any firewall.
A rogue DHCP server hands out the wrong gateway or DNS. DHCP snooping on the switch blocks server replies from untrusted ports.
Windows: ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew forces a new request.

SLAAC needs no server and no lease. The host builds a link-local FE80 address, sends a router solicitation, gets a router advertisement with the /64 prefix and gateway, adds its own interface identifier (EUI-64 or random), then runs duplicate address detection.

DHCPv6 is a separate protocol on UDP 546 (client) and 547 (server). It uses multicast because IPv6 has no broadcast. Exchange: solicit, advertise, request, reply. Reservations use a DUID instead of a MAC address.

rows: Hosts may use SLAAC for their address
Get the address from a DHCPv6 server (stateful, keeps leases)
Get other settings, such as DNS, from a DHCPv6 server (stateless)

blocks.text: SLAAC works but names do not resolve? The router advertisement needs the O flag and a stateless DHCPv6 server, or the RDNSS option. RA guard on access switches drops rogue router advertisements.

items: IP address management is the authoritative record of blocks, subnets, purposes and which addresses are assigned, reserved or free. It replaces the shared spreadsheet.
IPAM combined with DHCP and DNS is called DDI. One assignment can create the DHCP reservation and the forward and reverse DNS records, so they cannot drift apart.
Benefits: prevents duplicate addresses, shows subnet utilization for capacity planning, keeps an audit trail of assignments, and turns an IP address in an alert into a device, owner and location.

blocks.text: Clock drift never announces itself. Kerberos rejects tickets when clocks differ by more than 5 minutes, one-time passwords fail, certificates look expired, and logs from different devices cannot be lined up.

rows: Strata: 0 is the reference clock, 1 is attached to it, each hop adds 1, 16 means unsynchronized. Stratum is distance from the reference, not quality
Sub-microsecond accuracy. Switches act as boundary or transparent clocks and timestamp in hardware. Trading, broadcast, industrial and 5G
TCP 4460 for key setup, then UDP 123
TLS-established keys authenticate NTP. Classic NTP has almost no authentication

items: Use three or four sources so an outlier can be rejected. Two disagreeing servers cannot be resolved.
Best design: two or three internal servers sync to reliable outside sources, and every other device points only at them.
NTP distributes UTC. Time zones are a local setting.

title: Wi-Fi bands, standards, security and controllers (2.3)
summary: Pick channels that do not overlap, match Wi-Fi generations to their features, secure the wireless network with WPA3 and 802.1X, choose antennas, and separate autonomous from controller-managed access points.

rows: 11 channels in North America, 13 in much of Europe. Each channel is 20 MHz wide but centers sit 5 MHz apart, so only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap. Longest range, shared with microwave ovens and Bluetooth
IoT devices, older clients, coverage edges
About 25 non-overlapping 20 MHz channels. Shorter range, smaller cells. Channels roughly 52 to 144 share spectrum with radar and require DFS
Opened for unlicensed use in 2020. Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 only. Up to 59 channels at 20 MHz. Cleanest band, shortest range

items: Co-channel interference: two access points on one channel. Devices hear each other and take turns, so every client slows down.

Adjacent channel interference: access points on partly overlapping channels such as 3 and 5. They cannot decode each other, do not take turns, and both transmissions fail. It is worse than sharing a channel.
The correct 2.4 GHz plan reuses 1, 6 and 11 in a repeating pattern. Channels 1, 3, 5 and 7 perform worse than putting everything on channel 1.

DFS (802.11h): on radar channels the access point listens for 60 seconds before use, and must leave within 10 seconds of detecting radar and stay away 30 minutes. Every client on that AP drops at the same moment.

Channel bonding joins 20 MHz channels into 40, 80 or 160 MHz (320 MHz in Wi-Fi 7). Each doubling roughly doubles throughput but halves the channel count and lowers signal-to-noise ratio. Use 20 MHz on 2.4 GHz.
Regulatory domains set legal channels and power by country. A client from another region may not see every channel.
Band steering delays 2.4 GHz responses to push dual-band clients to 5 GHz. Aggressive steering can strand edge clients.

rows: First MIMO (multiple antennas). Up to about 600 Mbps
MU-MIMO serves several devices at once. Beamforming aims the signal at the client. About 3.5 Gbps
OFDMA, MU-MIMO in both directions, target wake time, BSS coloring, 1024-QAM. Up to 9.6 Gbps. Built for crowded places, not just speed
Same standard with a third, uncongested band
320 MHz channels, 4K-QAM, multi-link operation (one device uses two bands at once). Up to about 46 Gbps

items: Older generations: 802.11b (2.4 GHz, 11 Mbps), 802.11a (5 GHz, 54 Mbps), 802.11g (2.4 GHz, 54 Mbps).
OFDMA splits a channel into small resource units so one transmission carries data for many devices. It helps most with many small transmissions such as voice and IoT.
MU-MIMO uses separate spatial streams to talk to several devices at the same time.
Target wake time lets devices schedule when they wake, which saves battery.
BSS coloring tags frames so an access point can ignore a neighbor's traffic on the same channel.

sections.title: SSID, BSSID, ESSID and network types

rows: Network name users pick, up to 32 characters, case sensitive, not unique
Identifies one radio on one access point. It is the MAC address of that radio. An AP with 3 SSIDs on 2 bands advertises 6 BSSIDs
One SSID shared across many access points

items: Access points send beacon frames about 10 times a second. Listening for beacons is passive scanning. Sending probe requests is active scanning.
Roaming is a change of BSSID inside the same ESSID, so the user notices nothing.

Hiding the SSID adds no security. Beacons still go out with a blank name, and the name appears in clear text in probe and association frames. MAC filtering also fails because MAC addresses are unencrypted and easy to clone.
Every SSID is beaconed on every radio at the lowest data rate. Keep it to about three SSIDs per radio: corporate, guest, and one for devices that cannot do enterprise authentication.
Infrastructure mode: clients associate with access points, which bridge to the wired LAN. Ad hoc (IBSS): clients talk directly with no AP, which is a risk in an enterprise.
Mesh: access points relay traffic wirelessly to each other, with only root nodes wired. Each hop roughly halves throughput.
Point-to-point links use directional antennas between two fixed sites with line of sight. Point-to-multipoint serves several remote sites from one central site.

rows: RC4 with a short initialization vector. Key can be recovered in minutes. Obsolete
AES with CCMP. The acceptable baseline. Personal mode is exposed to offline guessing of a captured four-way handshake
Replaces the shared-key handshake with SAE. Each guess needs a live, rate-limited exchange, and forward secrecy protects recorded traffic. Transition mode lets older clients stay at WPA2 strength
Homes and small offices. No per-user identity. Changing it means touching every device
Supplicant (client), authenticator (AP) and RADIUS authentication server using EAP
Each user authenticates and gets unique keys. Identity in logs, one account can be revoked, per-user VLANs

items: Guest network: its own SSID mapped to its own VLAN. The firewall allows the internet and denies internal and management networks. Client isolation stops guests reaching each other. Use a separate DHCP scope with a short lease.
Captive portal: redirects first web traffic to a terms, login or voucher page. It controls admission only and encrypts nothing. For encryption without a passphrase use WPA3 enhanced open (OWE).
WPS: push-button or PIN setup. Convenient but weak. The PIN method is vulnerable to brute force.
Rogue access points and evil twins are unauthorized APs. A Wi-Fi analyzer or wireless controller can find them.
An antenna does not create signal. Gain (dBi) only reshapes where the existing energy goes. Every 3 dB roughly doubles power in the favored direction.
Omnidirectional: 360 degrees horizontally in a donut pattern, about 2 to 5 dBi. Default on ceiling APs. Weak directly above and below, so a high-gain omni is poor for multi-story buildings.
Semi-directional (patch, panel): 60 to 120 degree wedge, about 6 to 12 dBi. Corridors, aisles, and wall-mounted units facing inward.
Highly directional (Yagi, parabolic dish): beams of 10 to 25 degrees, about 15 to 30 dBi. Point-to-point links over long distances with careful aiming.
Raising transmit power in a many-AP deployment makes cells overlap more and creates contention. Reduce power and add APs instead.
Power is asymmetric: a ceiling AP may transmit at 100 mW while a phone sends about 15 mW. The client hears the AP but the AP may not hear the client.
Signal bars show RSSI. Performance depends on signal-to-noise ratio.

rows: One to three APs in a small office. Thirty means thirty configurations to keep in sync
AP is radio hardware plus a tunnel to the controller. Controller defines SSIDs, security and VLANs once
Larger sites. Controller runs radio resource management (channels and power), coordinates roaming. Deploy it redundantly

items: An access point is a layer 2 bridge between 802.11 and Ethernet. It does not route, assign addresses or perform NAT. It is usually powered by PoE.
A controller can be a rack appliance, a function inside one AP, or a cloud dashboard. User traffic may tunnel to it or break out locally.
Fast roaming uses 802.11r. Plan about 15 to 20 percent overlap between adjacent cells.
First question: can the client join at all, or does it join and perform badly? Cannot join points to configuration or authentication. Joins but slow points to signal, interference or capacity.

Cannot connect: check SSID, security type (WPA2 vs WPA3), password, RADIUS server reachability, and any MAC filter. If no networks show at all, check that the adapter is enabled and the driver is current.
Weak signal: distance, low power, and attenuation. Drywall and wood barely attenuate. Glass and concrete are moderate. Metal, brick and stone are significant.
Signal-to-noise ratio matters more than RSSI. A low ratio causes retries and drops.
Non-Wi-Fi interference on 2.4 GHz: microwave ovens, Bluetooth and cordless phones. A spectrum or Wi-Fi analyzer shows channel use and interference.
A wireless site survey and heat map reveal coverage gaps and guide AP placement. Adding APs without a channel plan often makes things worse.

Sticky client: clings to a distant AP. Fix with a minimum RSSI threshold on the AP and roughly 15 to 20 percent cell overlap. Mismatched security settings between APs sharing an SSID also break roaming.
Many healthy clients dropped at once can be a DFS radar event, or forged deauthentication frames from an attacker.
